Deeply nested JSX is hard to follow, and it usually means that part of the tree should be its own component. The outermost element has depth 0, its children depth 1, and so on. By default the rule reports an element deeper than 2.

Elements inside an expression in braces, such as `{more && <li />}` or the callback of `.map()`, start again at depth 0.

## Examples

Reported:

{/* bad */}
```jsx
const page = (
  <main>
    <section>
      <ul>
        <li>First</li>
      </ul>
    </section>
  </main>
);
```

Not reported:

{/* good */}
```jsx
const page = (
  <main>
    <section>
      <ItemList />
    </section>
  </main>
);
```

{/* good */}
```jsx
const page = (
  <main>
    <section>
      <ul>
        {items.map(item => <li key={item.id}>{item.title}</li>)}
        {more && <li>More</li>}
      </ul>
    </section>
  </main>
);
```

## Options

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `max` | `2` | The deepest level that is allowed. |

{/* bad {"options": [{"max": 1}]} */}
```jsx
const page = (
  <main>
    <section>
      <ItemList />
    </section>
  </main>
);
```

Moving part of the tree to a variable does not change its depth:

{/* bad {"options": [{"max": 1}]} */}
```jsx
const section = (
  <section>
    <ItemList />
  </section>
);

const page = <main>{section}</main>;
```
